Artificial Intelligence

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
....what is AI and how dangerous is it?

Unique Selling Point:
It is the technology of the 21st Century that will fundamentally change all our lives, and it is already happening.

Summary:
Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning

It is called the 4th industrial revolution and it is set to change the world as we know if completely. It is already changing the world. The previous ones were : Steam 1794, Electricity 1870, Information technology 1970.

AI will fundamentally change everything we do, from medicine to transport to energy and manufacturing. Many specialized jobs we know today, will soon become obsolete. Some see it as a massive advance for humankind, but others see it as a threat.


Further information:
Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
• It is called the 4th industrial revolution and it is set to change the world as we know if completely. It is already changing the world. The previous ones were : Steam 1794, Electricity 1870, Information technology 1970.
• Stephen Hawking, Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak, and many other big names in science and technology have recently expressed concern in the media and via open letters about the risks posed by AI.
• Others, like Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, argue that AI does not hold a threat. However, it is set to change the world as we know it. AI software will create significant business opportunities and societal value. Software companies will take up the mantle and charge ahead, pushing the boundaries of automation, search and social media. For example, virtual assistants or chatbots will offer expert assistance; smart robots or robot advisors in the fields on finance, insurance, legal, media and journalism will provide instantaneous research or findings; and within the healthcare field, AI software will assist with medical diagnosis and assistance. Other benefits include significantly improving efficiencies in R&D projects by reducing time to market, optimizing transport and supply chain networks, and improving governance by better decision-making processes. Already today, there are expert systems that can scan and share overviews of legal documents from obscure previous court rulings with lawyers within seconds, saving time and money. Autonomous driving, though still in the early stages, has also made tremendous progress; self-driving taxis were just recently launched in Singapore. And the list goes on, thus proving the inevitable ascendance of AI into our everyday lives. Dubbed a machine's brain, AI will likely power automation in sectors like autonomous vehicles and unmanned drones. AI is a technology that could change the world for the better. It can make medical procedures safer, increase productivity and boost the economy, or be used in applications to improve the quality of life for the disabled.
• But, AI is also a technology that comes with challenges, such as accountability, security, technological mistrust, and the displacement of human workers.
• Others argue that AI could be an existential threat to humanity, especially if it becomes self-aware. Hod Lipson of Columbia has claimed that he has done so already. They've created robots that decide for themselves how they want to walk; robots that develop a sense of what they look like; robots that are creative even robots that can, through trial and error, construct other robots just like themselves.
• Interviewees:
Prof Hod Lipson, Columbia Univeristy, Robotics and AI expert
Prof Vivienne Ming, Singularity University, world’s foremost AI creator
Prof. Tommie Meyer UCT, The Centre for Artificial Intelligence Research (CAIR) is a South African national research network that conducts foundational, directed and applied research into various aspects of Artificial Intelligence.
Prof Deshen Moodley, UCT

Filming two interviews at UCT

Prof. Hod Lipson

Prof. Deshen Moodley

Press Release:


It is called the 4th industrial revolution and it’s changing the world as we know it. From medicine to
transport and manufacturing – right down to the cellphone in your hand –artificial Intelligence is
taking over every aspect of our lives. Some experts see it as a massive advancement for
humankind, but others are raising the alarm. Carte Blanche analyses the impact of AI.

Script:


V/O:
When most people think about Artificial Intelligence or AI they think of the scary scenario where armies of evil killer robots conquer the world…… waging war on a few human survivors after the apocalypse…. destroying all mankind ……….to make room for the machines….
LINK 1:
This is an understanding of AI that we got from Hollywood, and it is a frightening prediction of a distant future, but few people realize artificial Intelligence has already arrived and it is already all around us, changing our lives.
V/O:
In New York City, at Columbia University Prof Hod Lipson is a robotics engineer, using Artificial Intelligence to control his creations.
Hod:
It basically means a collection of software that can imitate human intelligence, and that is a whole variety of activities
From perception to logic to lanning but really we are talkin about software that can emulate human intelligence.
V/O:
And the last year or two AI’s have become incredibly powerful, even creative, some even writing poetry.

they were the only ones left.
he had to be with me.
she had to be with him.
i had to do this.
i wanted to kill him.
i started to cry.
i turned to him.

LINK 2:
This poem was written by an AI programmed to do this. But it can do only this. It cannot, for example, also control a self-driving car.
V/O:
This means there is no single AI controlling everything, but rather there are literally millions of AI’s performing intelligent tasks, making our lives easier.
Hod:
Most people don’t realise that their voice recognition on their phones or the fact that they can know what the weather… whether it is going to rain tomorrow or not or the stock prices that govern their retirement are all determined by AI. Thye don’t see that and they think “where is the AI we see in movies?”. But really AI is everywhere.
V/O:
Social media platforms are examples of powerful AI’s. And AI is fast affecting every job in the world says Dr Vivienne Ming, a world renowned AI creator.
Vivienne:
Doctors, lawyer, scientists, all the way down to agricultural workers. So, for example, friends of mine have a company where there is this robot and in runs through the fields. It has little cameras and it can visually, kind of the way you and I do, nut it sees a much broader spectrum, it can visually distinguish the crops from the weeds, and with little millimetre precision jets of fertilizer can kill the weeds while fertilizing the crops. You get conventional scale organic farming without needing any people.
V/O:
And in all areas of human activity, jobs that can be automated will soon be taken over by AI.
Hod:
For example, high level jobs, for example a radiologist that looks at images and decides whether there is a pathology or not is a very highly paid job. That can go away very easily. AI is already doing better than doctors and teams of doctors in certain forms of diagnostics.
V/O:
And automated diagnoses will completely change the face of medicine.
LINK 3:
In the remotest place on earth somebody with a smart phone and access to the internet will be able to make sophisticated diagnoses without the help of specialists.
V/O:
And AI’s linked to robotic systems could begin to replace surgeons because, frankly, they are better. For example, here a robotic system is stitching the skin of a grape back together, made possible by AI.
Hod:
The same things has happened with pilots of air craft. You can see that the effort to fly a plane has dropped with increasing AI and so have the salaries of pilots.
V/O:
Prof Tommie Meyer at the University of Cape Town is the co-founder of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence Research and says AI’s are also incredibly good at processing data to make predictions, even in unlikely areas such as law.
Tommie:
There have been a couple of examples in the past year or so where AI algorithms were able to predict the outcome of court cases purely based on the data that was provided beforehand.

John:
Isn’t that extraordinary. Justice equals x plus y squared minus two.

Tommy:
Yes, in a sense it is a bit scary.
LINK 4:
All of this has become possible in the last few years because of the enormous strides made in computer technology. Computers have more computation power than ever before and can handle enormous amounts of data at lightning fast speeds.
V/O:
And computers and AI’s are not only programmed. They can also learn independently of humans and become better and better at what they do. This is a robot with a CPU, motors and legs, but has not been programmed to walk. It develops this ability all by itself. It learns. Newer AI’s are based on neural networks that resemble the human brain and learn even faster.
LINK:
Some say that by 2045 the technological singularity will be reached. – the point where super intelligent computers will surpass human intelligence and abruptly trigger runaway technological growth, and then the world will not be controlled by humans, but by machines.
V/O:
Elon Musk has for some time been warning against the unregulated development of AI.
Musk:
I keep sounding the alarm bell but till people see like robots going down the street and killing people they don’t know how to react because it seems so ethereal. AI is a fundamental existential risk for human civilization and I don’t think people fully appreciate that.
V/O:
However, there are others who are convinced AI does not pose any threat.
Zuckerberg:
With AI especially I am really optimistic. I think people who are naysayers and try to draw up these doomsday scenarios are… I don’t understand it, I think it is really negative and in some ways I actually think it is pretty irresponsible.
Link 6:
All the AI experts we spoke to for this story tend to side with Zuckerberg and says Elon Musk’s doomsday scenario is not a realistic threat.
Tommie:
The whole idea of robots or beings somehow becoming conscious on their own or self aware on their own and trying to take over the world. If at all, we are very, very far away.
V/O:
However, the consensus is that AI is rapidly changing the world in its entirety. So where does this leave South Africa? Prof. Deshen Moodley is also involved with the Centre for AI Research.
Deshen Moodley:
I think the phrase is “the train has already left the station”. What is happening is, the train is speeding up, and from a South African perspective actually need to make sure that we are on that train as it speeds up, and that is the concern. But it terms of our spend as a country on technology, on computer science, we are falling far behind.
V/O:
But elsewhere AI’s are being designed to link computers with the human brain this will augment our brain capacity and make us ten times or a hundred times smarter.

In just a year or two self-driven cars and aircraft will be more common – all controlled by AI ‘s.

And in cities of the future AI’s will monitor our health constantly – forecasting diseases and eradicating them before they even start.

And predictions are that AI controlled robotic systems in all shapes and sizes will very soon become part of our everyday lives, even in our homes.
LINK:
Nobody can for sure where AI will take us, but of one thing we can be sure – it will change our lives profoundly.
Vivienne:
The world has never changed as fast as it is changing today, and it will never be this slow again.
